# Reflection

## Where the agent was most reliable

Anywhere the answer could be checked mechanically. Pointer-order reasoning in
the rotations was exact: it could say *why* `x->parent` has to be read at line
113 before it is written at line 118, not just that the order works. Case
analysis on `insert_fixup` held up under four separate audits — the
black-height counting proof that a black uncle on the first iteration must be
NIL, the configuration handed from case 2 to case 3, the two-rotation bound,
and which line reseats `t->root`. I pushed on all four expecting one to
collapse and none did.

It was also good at the grinding, repeatable work I would have done badly by
hand: generating fifty-odd mutants of `src/rbtree.c`, compiling each against
the real test binary, and tabulating which test killed which. That is where
most of this project's actual findings came from, and none of them needed
insight so much as patience.

## Where it was least reliable

Claims about its own test coverage. Every single time it wrote a test and told
me what that test covered, it was over-confident, and mutation testing was the
only thing that settled it:

- `test_spec_zigzag` had a comment saying it forced the zig-zag case and
  caught a missed `t->root` update. It performed **zero rotations**.
- The eight-key figure fixture it replaced that with missed four case-2
  mutants, which only a three-key fixture catches.
- `tests/test_validate.c`'s "rule 4" case had never once tested rule 4.
- `rb_foreach` could have been handing every callback `NULL` where the value
  belongs and the entire suite would have stayed green, because every callback
  in the file starts with `(void)value`.
- `make test` could not detect a broken `rb_validate` at all: thirteen of
  fifteen mutants survived, including replacing the function body with
  `return 0`.

None of those are exotic. They are all the same failure: a test that runs and
passes, and never reaches the thing it is named after. An agent will describe
what a test *intends*. It cannot tell you what the test *exercises* unless you
make it break the code and watch.

Second, it is bad at knowing when its instruments are lying. It reported ten
mutants as "crashed before any labelled test" — that was stdout buffering
being discarded by the segfault, not a real result. It wrote a probe that
inserted `NULL` values and then checked `if (!rb_find(...))`, which reports
every key as lost, because `rb_find` returns the value. It caught both of
those only after I asked it to verify outputs rather than report them.

## One bug it introduced that I caught, and how

It proposed replacing the dead `test_spec_zigzag` with the keys `{50,20,35}`
and `{50,70,60}`, in a comment citing "Spec §3, Figure 4". Those keys do
rotate at the root, so the test would have passed and looked correct.

I caught it by not letting it cite a document it had not opened. I told it to
read the PDFs and check the alignment. Figures 4 and 5 turn out not to be an
insertion sequence at all — they start from a legal seven-node tree and insert
`25`. The original broken test had read the node labels off the figure and
treated them as an insert order, and the replacement inherited the same
mistake in a subtler form: three keys can only reach the fixup loop once, and
on the first iteration a black uncle is provably always NIL. The configuration
the figure is *about* — a real black uncle with subtrees hanging off it — is
unreachable in three keys.

The lesson generalises past this bug. The agent's diagnosis was right and its
fix was plausible and wrong, and the thing that separated them was a primary
source sitting in `~/Downloads` that nothing in the repo pointed at.

## The thing about C that most surprised the Java programmer I was two weeks ago

That a function's return value can be structurally incapable of answering the
question you are asking it.

`rb_find` returns the value, or `NULL` if the key is absent. In Java I would
reach for `containsKey` without thinking, and the ambiguity would never come
up. In C the signature is frozen in Appendix A and there is no second channel:
a key stored with a `NULL` value and a key that is not there return exactly
the same thing. That is not a bug in the header, it is the contract. But it
bit me for real — a debugging probe inserted `NULL` payloads, checked the
result for truthiness, and cheerfully reported that six different mutants had
lost every key in the tree. Nothing was wrong. The question was unanswerable
and the answer looked definite.

The close runner-up is the same shape: consequences that are invisible until
something else goes wrong. A reused stack buffer is why the tree has to copy
every key — store the pointer and you have stored a buffer that gets
overwritten on the next loop iteration, and nothing tells you until much
later. A segfault discards buffered `stdout`, so a crash does not merely fail,
it deletes the evidence of where it failed. Java would have flushed on the way
out with a stack trace attached.

Coming from a language where the runtime narrates your mistakes back to you,
the adjustment is not that C is harder. It is that C is *quiet*. The
verification tooling — ASan, valgrind, and the mutation sweeps — is not
paranoia bolted onto the assignment. It is the narration, added back by hand.

# Reflection

## Where the agent was most reliable

Anything I could check mechanically. I audited `insert_fixup` four separate
times and it held up every time, including the black-height proof that a black
uncle on the first iteration has to be NIL, and the two-rotation bound. When I
asked which line reseats `t->root` it pointed at `src/rbtree.c:115` instead of
guessing. It was also good at the boring repeatable work, like building fifty
mutants of `src/rbtree.c` and tabulating which test killed which.

## Where it was least reliable

Claims about its own test coverage. `test_spec_zigzag` had a comment saying it
forced the zig-zag case, however it did zero rotations. `make test` could not
detect a broken `rb_validate` at all, and 13 of 15 mutants survived including
one that replaced the whole function body with `return 0`. The agent will tell
you what a test intends. It cannot tell you what the test actually exercises
unless you break the code on purpose and watch which test dies.

## One bug it introduced that I caught

It wanted to replace the dead `test_spec_zigzag` with keys `{50,20,35}`, and
cited Figure 4 in the comment. Those keys do rotate, so the test would have
passed and looked right. I caught it by telling it to actually read the PDFs
instead of citing them. Figures 4 and 5 are not an insert sequence at all,
they start from a legal seven node tree and insert 25. Three keys only run the
fixup loop once, and on the first pass a black uncle is always NIL, so the
case the figure is about cannot happen in three keys.

## The thing about C that surprised me

I did take a C++ course a while ago so pointers were not new, however doing it
from scratch is a lot more complicated. Java has nodes too, but in C it is
much more direct and you manage the tree explicitly. What I did not see coming
is that a return value can be incapable of answering the question you are
asking. `rb_find` returns the value, or NULL if the key is absent, so a key
stored with a NULL value and a key that is not there look exactly the same. In
Java I would use `containsKey` without thinking about it. That cost me real
time on a probe that told me six mutants had lost every key when nothing was
wrong.

  `return 0`.

These are all the same failure. A test runs, it passes, and it never reaches
the thing it is named after. The agent will tell you what a test intends.
However it cannot tell you what the test actually exercises unless you break
the code on purpose and watch which test dies.

It is also bad at noticing when its own instruments are lying. It reported ten
mutants as crashing before any labelled test. That was just stdout buffering
getting thrown away by the segfault. It wrote a probe that inserted NULL
values and then checked `if (!rb_find(...))`, which reports every key as lost.
Both times it only caught it after I made it verify the output instead of
reporting it.

## One bug it introduced that I caught

It wanted to replace the dead `test_spec_zigzag` with keys `{50,20,35}` and
`{50,70,60}`, and cited Figure 4 in the comment. Those keys do rotate at the
root, so the test would have passed and looked right.

I caught it by not letting it cite a document it never opened. I told it to
read the PDFs and check. Figures 4 and 5 are not an insert sequence at all.
They start from a legal seven node tree and insert 25. The original broken
test had read the node labels off the figure and used them as an insert order,
and the replacement had the same mistake in a quieter form. Three keys only
run the fixup loop once, and on the first pass a black uncle is always NIL. So
the thing the figure is actually about, a real black uncle with subtrees under
it, cannot happen in three keys.

Its diagnosis was right and its fix was wrong, and what separated them was a
PDF sitting in my Downloads folder that nothing in the repo pointed at.

## The thing about C that surprised me

I did take a C++ course a while ago so pointers were not new, however doing it
from scratch is a lot more complicated. Java has nodes too, but in C it is
much more direct. You manage the tree explicitly and nobody cleans up after
you.

The part I did not see coming is that a return value can be incapable of
answering the question you are asking it. `rb_find` returns the value, or NULL
if the key is not there. In Java I would use `containsKey` without thinking
about it. In C the signature is frozen in Appendix A and there is no second
channel, so a key stored with a NULL value and a key that is absent return the
exact same thing. That is not a bug in the header. That is the contract.

It cost me real time. A debugging probe inserted NULL payloads, checked the
result for truthiness, and told me six different mutants had lost every key in
the tree. Nothing was wrong. The question could not be answered and the answer
still looked definite.

The other surprise is the same shape. A reused stack buffer is why the tree
has to copy every key, because if you store the pointer you have stored
something that gets overwritten on the next loop. A segfault throws away
buffered stdout, so a crash does not just fail, it deletes the evidence of
where it failed.

Coming from Java the adjustment is not that C is harder. It is that C does not
tell you anything. ASan and valgrind and the mutation sweeps are not extra
paranoia on top of the assignment. They are the part Java was doing for me,
put back by hand.
